title: Research Bite #15: Exploring the Foundations of Explicit Instruction
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #15 covers Anita Archer and Charles Hughes' “Exploring the Foundations of Explicit Instruction,” a systematic account of explicit instruction as a structured teaching methodology built around clear explanation, demonstration, and supported practice. Drawing on research from both general and special education, Archer and Hughes lay out a detailed set of design principles: focus instruction on genuinely critical content rather than everything a curriculum could cover; sequence skills logically, teaching easier and higher-frequency skills before harder or rarer ones and separating similar skills to avoid confusion; break complex skills into small instructional steps to manage working-memory demand, then resynthesize them into the whole; open lessons with a clear statement of goals; review prior knowledge before introducing new material; model skills with step-by-step demonstration; use precise, unambiguous language; and provide a deliberate mix of examples and non-examples to mark the boundaries of when a skill applies. The paper also stresses process elements often missing from discussions of explicit instruction — brisk pacing, frequent student responses, close monitoring, immediate corrective feedback, and distributed, cumulative practice for retention. Barton distills the paper's overall claim into a single line that anchors the whole piece: many students need explicit instruction in order to learn and apply academic skills, and the paper functions as a practical checklist for what doing that well actually requires.
points: The paper functions as a detailed, checklist-style operationalization of explicit instruction — moving well beyond the general “tell, show, practice” shorthand into specific design moves like sequencing, chunking, and example/non-example selection.

The sequencing principles (easier before harder, high-frequency before rare, similar skills kept apart) give curriculum designers concrete ordering rules rather than a vague call to “build up gradually.”

Providing both examples and non-examples is highlighted as essential for establishing the actual boundaries of a skill or concept — teaching only positive examples leaves students unable to recognize when a rule doesn't apply.

Process elements — brisk pacing, frequent student responses, close monitoring, and immediate corrective feedback — are treated as core components of explicit instruction, not optional classroom-management add-ons layered on top of good content delivery.

Distributed and cumulative practice is built into the model from the start as the mechanism for retention and automaticity, tying this paper directly to the spacing and retrieval-practice research covered elsewhere in the series.
quotes: The text explores explicit instruction as a systematic and effective teaching methodology. It details the elements and underlying principles of explicit instruction, emphasizing its structured approach with clear explanations, demonstrations, and supported practice.

Focusing instruction on critical content by teaching skills, strategies, vocabulary, and concepts that will empower students in the future and match their instructional needs. Teachers can examine their curriculum, select the most critical skills and objectives, and discard or deemphasize the less critical ones.

Sequencing skills logically by teaching easier skills before harder ones, high-frequency skills before less frequent ones, ensuring mastery of prerequisites, and separating similar skills to avoid confusion.
Providing a range of examples and non-examples to establish the boundaries of when and when not to apply a skill, strategy, concept, or rule.
Providing immediate affirmative and corrective feedback to students about the accuracy of their responses to ensure high rates of success and reduce the likelihood of practicing errors.
Providing distributed and cumulative practice with multiple opportunities to practice a skill over time, addressing retention and automaticity.
Many students need explicit instruction in order to learn and apply academic skills
